title: Transient corium stratification and heat focusing
open: What is the maximum heat load a reactor vessel wall experiences while corium is still arriving, absorbing structural material, and exchanging species between its oxide and metal layers — and can transient stratification or inversion produce peak loads that steady-state configurations miss?
status: Carénini et al. (2025) compared eight IAEA benchmark cases and documented remaining thermochemistry, heavy-metal-layer, debris-melting, and heat-transfer discrepancies after decades of retention research.
solved_when: A predictive capability bounds the maximum vessel-wall heat loading during transient pool formation, including progressive melt arrival, incorporation of structural material, and interlayer species exchange, and resolves whether transient stratification or inversion yields peaks beyond steady-state configurations.
why: Demonstrating in-vessel melt retention requires bounding transient heat loads; a steady-state analysis that misses transient peaks could falsely conclude the vessel survives.
key_works: L. Carénini et al. (2025), *IVMR modelling with transient effects during molten pool formation and stabilization—Outcomes from models’ comparison performed in the IAEA CRP J46002*, [DOI:10.1016/j.anucene.2025.111365](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anucene.2025.111365).

title: Directional corium–concrete erosion
open: Can we predict, from melt composition, concrete chemistry, gas generation, and crust structure, how concrete erosion by molten corium splits over time between lateral and downward directions? A successful model would reproduce this evolving directional split across siliceous and carbonate-bearing concretes, under both dry and flooded reactor conditions.
status: The OECD NEA MCCI programme and its 2017 state-of-the-art synthesis report established substantial integral experimental evidence, but orientation-dependent erosion and extrapolation among concrete compositions remain sources of uncertainty (OECD NEA, 2017, [*State-of-the-Art Report on Molten Corium Concrete Interaction and Ex-Vessel Molten Core Coolability*](https://cms.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_19746/state-of-the-art-report-on-molten-corium-concrete-interaction-and-ex-vessel-molten-core-coolability)).
solved_when: A predictive treatment of the erosion geometry is validated across siliceous and carbonate-bearing concretes under dry and flooded conditions, capturing orientation-dependent erosion without ad hoc recalibration for each composition.
why: The erosion geometry sets the cooling surfaces available and the progression of structural attack on the containment basemat, so it directly governs ex-vessel coolability and containment integrity assessments.
key_works: OECD NEA (2017), [*State-of-the-Art Report on Molten Corium Concrete Interaction and Ex-Vessel Molten Core Coolability*](https://cms.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_19746/state-of-the-art-report-on-molten-corium-concrete-interaction-and-ex-vessel-molten-core-coolability).

title: Recombiner performance in chemically complex atmospheres
open: Can we predict the hydrogen removal rate of a passive catalytic recombiner when the accident atmosphere is chemically complex — mixed gases, aerosols, limited oxygen, and catalyst poisons — and can we describe how the catalyst degrades and recovers as that atmosphere changes over time?
status: The THEMIS project (OECD NEA and Becker Technologies, 2020–2024) completed targeted tests by 2023 and an integral aerosol–recombiner interaction test in 2024; transferring results across mixtures and exposure histories remains open.
solved_when: A validated predictive capability for recombiner removal rates exists under mixed gases, aerosols, oxygen limitation, and catalyst poisoning, including validated degradation and recovery behavior across changing accident atmospheres and transferability of results across mixtures and exposure histories.
why: Catalytic mitigation of hydrogen must function in the very atmosphere it is helping to control; without predictive capability under these conditions, recombiner performance in a real severe accident is uncertain.
key_works: OECD NEA and Becker Technologies (2020–2024), [*THAI Experiments on Mitigation measures… (THEMIS)*](https://oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_58863/thai-experiments-on-mitigation-measures-and-source-term-issues-to-support-analysis-and-further-improvement-of-severe-accident-management-measures-themis-project).

title: Organic iodine from aged containment surfaces
open: Can we predict how much organic iodine forms on — and is destroyed by — aged painted containment surfaces under irradiation, varying humidity, and chemical contaminants? A successful theory must resolve surface-layer, pore, and bulk-water reactions well enough that kinetic parameters transfer between coatings.
status: BIP phases through 2019 measured adsorption, desorption, and organic-iodide production (OECD NEA and Canadian Nuclear Laboratories, 2007–2019, [*Behaviour of Iodine Project (BIP)*](https://oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_24819/behaviour-of-iodine-project-bip)). Paint aging and confident reactor-scale extrapolation remained explicit programme targets.
solved_when: A predictive model exists that reproduces organic-iodine formation and destruction across coatings under the specified conditions (irradiation, humidity changes, chemical contamination) with kinetics transferable between coatings, enabling confident reactor-scale extrapolation.
why: Organic iodine can be harder to retain than other iodine forms, so unquantified production from aged surfaces undermines source-term estimates for severe accidents.
key_works: OECD NEA and Canadian Nuclear Laboratories (2007–2019), [*Behaviour of Iodine Project (BIP)*](https://oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_24819/behaviour-of-iodine-project-bip).

title: Species-resolved aerosol pool scrubbing
open: Can we predict, species by species, how much of each aerosol — by particle size and chemical form — is retained as bubbles rise through a water pool during a severe-accident transient? Such a prediction requires coupling bubble breakup, hygroscopic growth, dissolution, and re-entrainment into a validated model that goes beyond a single aggregate decontamination factor.
status: The OECD NEA/Becker Technologies THEMIS project (2020–2024) completed pool-scrubbing experiments and a benchmark by its 2024 closeout, but transfer among mixtures, bubble populations, and evolving chemistry remains incomplete.
solved_when: A model exists that resolves retention as a function of aerosol size and chemical species during transients, accounts for the coupled physics of breakup, hygroscopic growth, dissolution, and re-entrainment, and is validated against experimental data rather than an aggregate decontamination factor alone.
why: The least-retained fraction of the aerosol can dominate the airborne activity released, so aggregate retention factors can badly understate the source term.
key_works: OECD NEA and Becker Technologies (2020–2024), [*THAI Experiments on Mitigation measures… (THEMIS)*](https://oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_58863/thai-experiments-on-mitigation-measures-and-source-term-issues-to-support-analysis-and-further-improvement-of-severe-accident-management-measures-themis-project).

title: Gas-fast-reactor heat removal after depressurization
subfield: Integrated reactor systems and power conversion
open: Can a gas-cooled fast reactor reliably remove decay heat after a depressurization event that coincides with loss of normal electrical support, once realistic flow resistance and degraded equipment performance are accounted for? Formally, the goal is an experimental and analytical demonstration that decay-heat removal remains assured under these combined, degraded conditions.
status: Decay-heat removal after depressurization has been a central GFR issue since the 2002 Generation IV roadmap. ALLEGRO analyses and experiments have advanced, with Bali and Mayer's 2025 investigation of decay-heat removal systems in the ALLEGRO helium-cooled fast reactor supplying a recent partial result.
solved_when: Decay-heat removal for a gas-cooled fast reactor is demonstrated — experimentally and analytically — to remain reliable after simultaneous loss of pressure and loss of normal electrical support, with realistic flow resistance and degraded equipment included in the demonstration.
why: This capability determines whether the fast-spectrum helium-cooled concept can satisfy its safety case at all; without credible depressurized decay-heat removal, the GFR concept does not stand.
key_works: Stainsby et al. (2009), *Gas Cooled Fast Reactor Research and Development in the European Union*, [DOI:10.1155/2009/238624](https://doi.org/10.1155/2009/238624); Bali and Mayer (2025), [*Investigation of decay heat removal systems in the ALLEGRO helium-cooled fast reactor*](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0029549325001293).

title: Quantifying digital common-cause failure
subfield: Monitoring, control, operations, and probabilistic safety
open: Can we produce defensible quantitative bounds on the probability that nominally independent digital protection channels fail together — and can those bounds be grounded in measurable diversity? The question is to estimate common-cause failure probabilities for channels that share specifications, tools, suppliers, or development assumptions, and to validate whether proposed diversity metrics actually predict independence in practice.
status: The NRC's 2010 diversity-strategy report (Wood et al. (2010), [*Diversity Strategies for Nuclear Power Plant Instrumentation and Control Systems*](https://www.ornl.gov/publication/diversity-strategies-nuclear-power-plant-instrumentation-and-control-systems-0), NUREG/CR-7007) provides architectures and assessment foundations, but credible quantitative probabilities for rare shared software defects remain unresolved.
solved_when: A method exists that yields credible, defensible failure-probability bounds for diverse digital protection channels with shared digital infrastructure, validated by evidence that proposed diversity measures predict actual independence of channels.
why: Without it, nominal redundancy in digital safety systems systematically overstates reliability, since channels that appear independent can fail from a shared software defect.
key_works: Wood et al. (2010), [*Diversity Strategies for Nuclear Power Plant Instrumentation and Control Systems*](https://www.ornl.gov/publication/diversity-strategies-nuclear-power-plant-instrumentation-and-control-systems-0), NUREG/CR-7007.

title: Safe industrial-heat interfaces across plant boundaries
subfield: Electricity systems, industrial heat, hydrogen, and water
open: Can interfaces be qualified that isolate a nuclear heat source from the chemical hazards of an industrial process plant, while still tolerating the rapid demand changes typical of industrial operations? In particular, can it be demonstrated that process-plant upsets do not invalidate the assumptions underlying reactor protection?
status: HTTR experience and JAEA's 2020 cogeneration work (Sato, Aoki, Ohashi, and Yan, 2020, *Research and development for safety and licensing of HTGR cogeneration system*) establish the design and licensing foundations; broader industrial integration still requires application-specific validation and commercial demonstration.
solved_when: An interface design is qualified that isolates nuclear heat sources from industrial chemical hazards, tolerates rapid demand changes, and is shown — through application-specific validation and commercial demonstration — to preserve reactor protection assumptions under process-plant upsets.
why: It unlocks the supply of nuclear steam and high-temperature heat to manufacturing processes, extending nuclear energy beyond electricity into industrial heat markets.
key_works: Sato, Aoki, Ohashi, and Yan (2020), [*Research and development for safety and licensing of HTGR cogeneration system*](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0029549319305242).

title: Accelerator availability for subcritical power systems
subfield: Space, marine systems, research reactors, and accelerator-driven systems
open: Can an accelerator-driven civilian system be made to operate usefully for a sustained campaign despite realistic beam interruptions, recovery transients, target degradation, and thermal cycling?
status: The problem has been pursued for decades. MYRRHA's staged accelerator development work places strong emphasis on reliability, and EU programmes (including the MAX consortium, 2011–2014) have compared availability requirements against operating evidence; a complete availability demonstration remains open. Key references: SCK CEN, [*MYRRHA linear accelerator*](https://www.myrrha.be/about-myrrha/myrrha-linear-accelerator); EU MAX consortium (2011–2014), [*MYRRHA Accelerator eXperiment*](https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/269565/reporting).
solved_when: An accelerator-driven system demonstrates integrated availability — beam interruptions, recovery times, target lifetime, and thermal cycling all within operational limits — over a representative campaign, with quantitative targets set by the availability requirements established in EU programme comparisons with operating evidence.
why: It determines whether the promised transmutation and irradiation benefits of accelerator-driven systems survive real-world interruptions and maintenance demands.
key_works: SCK CEN, [*MYRRHA linear accelerator*](https://www.myrrha.be/about-myrrha/myrrha-linear-accelerator); EU MAX consortium (2011–2014), [*MYRRHA Accelerator eXperiment*](https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/269565/reporting).

title: High-burnup cladding after decades of thermal history
open: Can we predict the residual ductility and fracture resistance of high-burnup cladding once it has passed through a realistic drying, cooling, and storage history measured in decades rather than months? In formal terms, the goal is a validated predictive capability whose blind forecasts, across cladding alloys, match measurements on genuinely aged irradiated material.
status: NWTRB's 2021 review of the DOE research program on commercial high-burnup spent nuclear fuel performance during extended storage and transportation identified gaps in representativeness and in integration. Current validation rests on short specimens and accelerated histories, which provide incomplete evidence for long-term behavior.
solved_when: Blind predictions of residual ductility and fracture resistance, made before testing, agree with measurements on aged irradiated cladding specimens across the commercial cladding alloys, for histories representative of actual drying, cooling, and storage.
why: Without it, arguments for extending storage durations and for subsequent handling, transport, and disposal of high-burnup fuel rest on extrapolation rather than demonstrated material performance.
key_works: NWTRB (2021), [*Evaluation of the Department of Energy’s Research Program to Examine the Performance of Commercial High Burnup Spent Nuclear Fuel During Extended Storage and Transportation*](https://www.nwtrb.gov/our-work/reports/evaluation-of-the-department-of-energy's-research-program-to-examine-the-performance-of-commercial-high-burnup-spent-nuclear-fuel-during-extended-storage-and-transportation-(july-2021)).

title: Site-specific canister corrosion forecasting
open: Can we forecast how long a dry-storage canister will last at a specific site, starting from local weather data and measurements of its actual surface condition? Concretely, this requires predicting the coupled distributions of chloride deposition, deliquescence and wetting events, pit initiation, and subsequent crack growth, and validating the resulting remaining-life estimates at both coastal and inland installations.
status: The underlying laboratory mechanisms and deposition models exist. Suffield et al.'s 2023 report (posted 2024, PNNL-34772) developed thermal and deposition modeling for heated canisters, while describing the coastal field demonstration itself as still prospective.
solved_when: A calibrated model driven by site weather and measured canister surfaces reproduces observed chloride deposition, wetting, pit-initiation, and crack-growth distributions, and yields validated remaining-life predictions across coastal and inland installations.
why: It converts canister inspection and maintenance from schedule-based guesswork into evidence-based decisions, allowing inspection intervals to be set and maintenance targeted where degradation actually progresses.
key_works: S. R. Suffield et al. (2023), [*Thermal and Deposition Modeling Update for the Canister Deposition Field Demonstration*](https://www.pnnl.gov/publications/thermal-and-deposition-modeling-update-canister-deposition-field-demonstration), PNNL-34772.

title: Valid acceleration of waste-glass durability tests
open: Which accelerated test conditions genuinely preserve the mechanisms that govern long-term radionuclide release from waste glass, and can we state transfer rules and uncertainty bounds that connect laboratory tests, natural analogues, and repository conditions for specified glass families?
status: Standard durability methods date to the 1980s. Thorpe et al. (2021) document methodological progress over forty years of standard-method durability assessment and composition-dependent glass responses, but a universal acceleration factor remains unjustified.
solved_when: For specified glass families, a validated set of acceleration conditions exists with explicit transfer rules and quantified uncertainty bounds linking accelerated tests to repository-relevant release behavior, justified mechanistically rather than by a universal acceleration factor.
why: It would let glass qualification proceed on a defensibly shortened timeline without losing the chemistry that actually controls long-term release, replacing decades-old standard methods with acceleration whose validity is demonstrated.
key_works: C. L. Thorpe et al. (2021), *Forty Years of Durability Assessment of Nuclear Waste Glass by Standard Methods*, [DOI:10.1038/s41529-021-00210-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-021-00210-4).

title: Dilatant gas migration through clay barriers
open: Can we predict how gas moves through a clay barrier that dilates under pressure — when a pathway opens, how far it propagates, when it reseals, and how it couples to water flow — under realistic repository stress histories? The target is a single predictive model that reproduces independent laboratory and large-scale experiments without retuning its mechanisms from test to test.
status: DECOVALEX-2019 compared modeling approaches for this problem, and DECOVALEX-2023 Task B extended the work toward larger experiments. Gas-pathway transferability between tests remains unresolved.
solved_when: A model of dilatant gas migration predicts breakthrough, pathway creation, resealing, and coupled water movement under realistic clay-barrier stress histories, and reproduces independent laboratory and large-scale experiments without retuning mechanisms for each test.
why: It constrains the pressure and transport effects of gases generated within a geological repository, which governs whether engineered clay barriers can retain their sealing function over time.
key_works: DECOVALEX (2019–2023), [*DECOVALEX-2023 Task B: Gas Transport in Clay*](https://decovalex.org/past-phases/D-2023/task-b).

title: Seawater uranium recovery with favourable full lifecycle performance
open: Can uranium be recovered from seawater in a system that remains attractive once everything is counted — material lifetime, regeneration, energy use, marine impacts, and full costs? The goal is a demonstration at a stated scale with complete mass, energy, and cost balances from repeated real-seawater operation.
status: The problem has been investigated for decades. Abney et al.'s 2017 review ([DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00355](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00355)) documents adsorbent and marine-testing progress, but industrial lifecycle performance remains beyond what laboratory uptake capacities demonstrate.
solved_when: A sustained real-seawater recovery demonstration at a stated scale is reported, with complete lifecycle balances — adsorbent lifetime and regeneration, energy use, marine environmental impacts, and full costs — showing favourable overall performance.
why: A solution would diversify uranium resources while establishing the actual environmental tradeoffs of seawater extraction rather than laboratory uptake capacities alone.
key_works: C. W. Abney, R. T. Mayes, T. Saito, and S. Dai (2017), *Materials for the Recovery of Uranium from Seawater*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00355](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00355).

title: Convergent selection of fission collective coordinates
open: Can we find a principled, error-controlled rule for selecting the collective coordinates — deformation, neck, pairing, and intrinsic degrees of freedom — used in reduced descriptions of fission, and prove that observable distributions converge as the omitted coordinates are restored?
status: The problem predates modern density-functional calculations and remains explicitly open in the 2020 fission-theory roadmap (M. Bender et al. (2020), *Future of Nuclear Fission Theory*, [arXiv:2005.10216](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.10216)). Successful fits using a few coordinates do not establish that the reduction preserves all relevant fission branches.
solved_when: A coordinate-selection criterion is given whose approximation error is quantified, and observable distributions (e.g., fragment yields, energies) are demonstrably converged upon restoration of the omitted coordinates.
why: Such a criterion would let us tell genuine physical predictions of fission observables from artifacts introduced by an arbitrary choice of shape space.
key_works: M. Bender et al. (2020), *Future of Nuclear Fission Theory*, [arXiv:2005.10216](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.10216).

title: Microscopic capture–fission branching without phenomenological widths
open: Can the competition between neutron capture and fission be computed directly from microscopic many-body dynamics, with a single common normalization across both channels? That is, reproduce the observed capture-to-fission branching ratios over an energy interval and identify which missing configurations or interactions dominate any remaining discrepancies.
status: Uzawa and Hagino's 2025 nonequilibrium Green-function calculation [arXiv:2504.01572](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01572) added proton–neutron interactions and relaxed a seniority restriction, but still underestimated the experimental fission-to-capture branching ratio by about an order of magnitude.
solved_when: A microscopic calculation with a common normalization reproduces experimental capture–fission branching ratios across an energy interval, and the dominant sources of discrepancy (missing configurations or interactions) are identified.
why: It tests whether reaction probabilities can emerge from microscopic dynamics rather than from independently fitted phenomenological channel widths.
key_works: K. Uzawa and K. Hagino (2025), *A microscopic calculation of fission cross sections with the non-equilibrium Green function method*, [arXiv:2504.01572](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01572).

title: Converged microscopic joint fragment distributions
open: Can a microscopic theory predict the full joint distribution of fission fragment charge, mass, and total kinetic energy — including covariances and rare branches — and show that this prediction converges as the number of microscopic trajectories grows? The goal is a demonstrably converged joint distribution validated on reactions not used in calibration.
status: Li et al. (2025) coherently combined 25 time-dependent trajectories for a realistic fission application, advancing beyond mean trajectories but not establishing convergence for all joint observables. [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.111.L051302](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.111.L051302)
solved_when: The predicted joint distribution of fragment charge, mass, and total kinetic energy, with covariances and rare branches, exhibits demonstrable convergence in the number of microscopic trajectories, and the result is validated on reactions excluded from calibration.
why: Marginal distributions can agree while the correlations needed for radiation predictions remain wrong; only a converged joint distribution guarantees those correlations are right.
key_works: B. Li et al. (2025), *Microscopic model for yields and total kinetic energy in nuclear fission*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.111.L051302](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.111.L051302).

title: Observable-independent definition of nuclear scission
open: Can nuclear scission be defined in a way that does not depend on an arbitrary choice of observable — so that the point and manner of fragment separation is a property of the state itself? Formally, the goal is a definition of fragment separation under which predicted fragment masses, excitation energies, and their post-scission interactions converge independently of arbitrary neck-density thresholds, and which reconciles localization-based and dynamical definitions in benchmark calculations.
status: Younes and Gogny's 2011 quantum-localization treatment [W. Younes and D. Gogny (2011), *Nuclear Scission and Quantum Localization*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.107.132501] clarified the separation of fragment wave functions, but a universally validated prescription spanning static, collective, and real-time calculations has not followed.
solved_when: A prescription for defining fragment separation exists that is validated across static, collective, and real-time calculations, yields convergent predictions of fragment masses, excitation energies, and interactions without dependence on arbitrary neck-density thresholds, and reproduces the localization-based and dynamical definitions in common benchmark calculations.
why: A shifting scission surface can change the inferred fragment properties even when the underlying nuclear state is the same, so fragment observables inherit the arbitrariness of the definition rather than reflecting the physics.
key_works: W. Younes and D. Gogny (2011), *Nuclear Scission and Quantum Localization*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.107.132501](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.107.132501).

title: Experimental separation of scission neutrons
open: Can an experiment cleanly isolate the neutrons emitted at the moment of neck rupture in fission, distinguishing them from the neutrons evaporated later by the accelerating fragments? The goal is an experimentally constrained scission-neutron spectrum and angular distribution that remains robust under alternative detector-response and fragment-emission models.
status: The existence of the scission-neutron mechanism has been debated for decades. Abdurrahman et al. (2023) supplied microscopic predictions of neck rupture and scission neutrons; a discriminating experimental extraction of this component remains the relevant open test.
solved_when: A scission-neutron component is extracted with its spectrum and angular distribution constrained by experiment, and the inferred component is shown to survive reasonable variations of the detector-response model and of the fragment-evaporation emission model.
why: Without a separated scission component, interpretations of prompt-neutron spectra and correlations carry an uncontrolled bias from this unresolved contribution.
key_works: I. Abdurrahman, M. Kafker, A. Bulgac, and I. Stetcu (2023), *Neck Rupture and Scission Neutrons in Nuclear Fission*, [arXiv:2307.13132](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13132).

title: Genuine three-heavy-fragment fission probability
open: Is true three-heavy-fragment fission of heavy nuclei — collinear tripartition into three medium-mass fragments — a reproducible decay channel, and if so, how often does it occur? A satisfactory answer should pin down its probability or a robust upper limit, with independent coincidence measurements that exclude binary-fission backgrounds and detector ambiguities.
status: The channel remains disputed. Jaganathen and Skalski (2025) predict strong dynamical suppression, with model-dependent upper estimates around \(10^{-8}\)–\(10^{-11}\) per binary decay for studied systems; this is not an impossibility proof ([arXiv:2506.22534](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22534)).
solved_when: Either an independent experimental confirmation establishes the probability of genuine tripartition as a nuclear decay channel, or theory and experiment jointly set a robust upper limit consistent with the dynamical suppression estimates, which currently lie around \(10^{-8}\)–\(10^{-11}\) per binary decay for the studied systems.
why: It probes how a nucleus chooses among competing fragmentation topologies, testing the limits of microscopic fission dynamics in a regime where binary decay overwhelmingly dominates.
key_works: Y. Jaganathen and J. Skalski (2025), *Suppression of genuine tripartition in heavy nuclei: A self-consistent perspective*, [arXiv:2506.22534](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22534).
aliases: Collinear cluster tripartition; genuine ternary fission.

title: Fragment excitation sharing and quantum entanglement
open: Can theory predict how excitation energy is shared between fission fragments as a function of fragment mass, including its fluctuations, without empirical energy-partition functions — and can we design measurements that distinguish genuinely quantum-entangled fragment states from purely statistical descriptions? A sharp test of any such description is whether it reproduces observed neutron-multiplicity trends from first principles.
status: Energy-sharing prescriptions remain model dependent. Y. Qiang, J. Pei, and K. Godbey (2024), *Quantum Entanglement in Nuclear Fission* ([arXiv:2408.07375](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07375)), connected microscopic entanglement to the observed sawtooth structure, while showing that additional fluctuations affect predicted slopes.
solved_when: A microscopic theory reproduces the fragment-mass dependence and fluctuations of excitation-energy sharing and the observed neutron-multiplicity trends (including the sawtooth structure) without empirical energy-partition functions, and identifiable measurements are specified that can discriminate entanglement-based descriptions from statistical alternatives.
why: Excitation sharing controls which fragment emits neutrons and how much gamma energy follows, so a principled prediction directly constrains the emitted-neutron and gamma observables of fission rather than fitting them.
key_works: Y. Qiang, J. Pei, and K. Godbey (2024), *Quantum Entanglement in Nuclear Fission*, [arXiv:2408.07375](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07375).

title: Origin of primordial fragment angular momentum
open: When and by what mechanism — collective rotation or microscopic modes — do fission fragments acquire their angular momentum? A satisfactory answer must identify observables that can distinguish spins generated independently after scission from spins correlated through pre-scission dynamics, before neutron evaporation and gamma emission wash out the difference.
status: Wilson et al. (2021) measured weak final-spin correlations, motivating a post-scission interpretation. Microscopic calculations continue to investigate different primordial correlations; measured final distributions do not uniquely fix the mechanism.
solved_when: A microscopic (or equivalent) account identifies when fragment spins are generated and through which modes, and proposes or demonstrates observables that discriminate independent post-scission spin generation from correlated pre-scission dynamics.
why: Fragment spins govern gamma-decay cascades and isomer production, so fixing the generation mechanism directly impacts the prediction of decay heat, gamma spectra, and isotope yields.
key_works: J. N. Wilson et al. (2021), *Angular momentum generation in nuclear fission*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-021-03304-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03304-w).

title: Reconstructing pre-emission fragment spin correlations
open: Can the primordial spin correlations of fission fragments be reconstructed from measured neutron–gamma coincidences, given decay models whose uncertainties are independently constrained? In particular, which of these correlations are identifiable from decay observables, and which are irreversibly erased by unobserved emissions?
status: Stetcu et al. (2021) [arXiv:2108.04347](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.04347) showed that neutron and gamma emissions remove substantial angular momentum during fragment decay. Consequently, interpreting final gamma observables as direct measurements of primordial spin remains an unresolved inverse problem.
solved_when: A decay-model analysis of neutron and gamma coincidence data identifies which pre-emission spin correlations are recoverable and which are destroyed by unobserved emissions, with uncertainties on the inversion independently constrained, and the resulting reconstruction is shown to discriminate among candidate fission-spin mechanisms.
why: Without a reliable inversion, measured gamma observables cannot be taken as direct probes of primordial fragment spin, leaving competing fission-spin mechanisms impossible to adjudicate.
key_works: I. Stetcu et al. (2021), *Angular Momentum Removal by Neutron and γ-Ray Emissions during Fission Fragment Decays*, [arXiv:2108.04347](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.04347).

title: Odd–even yield staggering across excitation and odd nuclei
open: Can microscopic fission theory predict how the odd–even staggering of charge and neutron number in fission-product yields changes with excitation energy, and extend that prediction to fissioning nuclei that are themselves odd? A complete answer would incorporate quasiparticle blocking and broken-pair configurations so that isotope-resolved yields are reproduced for even and odd systems alike, without recourse to empirical staggering factors.
status: Verriere, Regnier, and Schunck (2021) showed that charge staggering can be recovered microscopically using particle-number projection, but a systematic combination of this with realistic odd-system dynamics and excitation-energy dependence remains incomplete.
solved_when: A microscopic calculation reproduces isotope-resolved fission-product yields — including charge and neutron-number staggering — across both even and odd fissioning nuclei and as a function of excitation energy, with no empirical staggering factors.
why: The fine odd–even structure of yields controls the inventories of individual radionuclides and their decay emissions, so getting it wrong distorts any downstream prediction of fission products.
key_works: M. Verriere, D. Regnier, and N. Schunck (2021), *Microscopic Calculation of Fission Product Yields with Particle Number Projection*, [arXiv:2102.02346](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02346).

title: Uranium-238 state-resolved inelastic-scattering closure
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Can the total neutron inelastic-scattering cross section of 238U be reconstructed by consistently combining measured gamma transitions, the unobserved cascade feeding, and direct neutron measurements? Success requires closing the gap between state-specific measurements and the total channel with a documented covariance treatment.
status: A high-priority data request has existed since 2008. Kerveno et al. (2021) supplied extensive neutron-induced gamma data for 238U(n,n′γ), but incomplete level schemes and reaction-model dependence still complicate reconstruction of the total channel.
solved_when: A consistent, covariance-documented 238U inelastic cross section is obtained that reconciles state-resolved gamma data with direct neutron measurements and accounts for unobserved cascades and incomplete level schemes.
why: Uranium inelastic scattering modifies fast-neutron spectra and affects the interpretation of irradiation experiments, so an unresolved cross section propagates error into any calculation using those spectra.
key_works: M. Kerveno et al. (2021), *Measurement of 238U(n,n′γ) cross section data and their impact on reaction models*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.104.044605](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.104.044605); OECD NEA, [HPRL request](https://cms.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_68811/92-u-238-n-inl).

title: Plutonium-239 capture normalization across energy regimes
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Can resonance-region and fast-energy measurements of 239Pu neutron capture be brought into mutual agreement within a single joint capture–fission evaluation that carries shared normalization uncertainties? Success means matching independent measurements without resorting to separate energy-dependent adjustments that mask real discrepancies.
status: Mosby et al. (2018) provided a unifying capture measurement from keV to MeV energies. The NEA capture request remains active, and improved coverage has not eliminated evaluation and normalization questions.
solved_when: A joint capture–fission evaluation retaining shared normalization uncertainties across the keV-to-MeV energy regimes reproduces the independent resonance-region and fast-energy capture measurements within their quoted uncertainties, with no energy-dependent normalization adjustments applied.
why: Capture competition governs isotope evolution and neutron balances in civilian fuel calculations, so unresolved normalization discrepancies propagate directly into reactor physics predictions.
key_works: S. Mosby et al. (2018), *Unifying measurement of 239Pu(n,γ) in the keV to MeV energy regime*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.97.041601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.97.041601).

title: Independently replicated plutonium-241 capture data
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Can the neutron-capture cross section of plutonium-241 be measured and independently replicated so that it no longer rests on a single decades-old dataset? Formally, this calls for a covariance-bearing evaluation of 241Pu capture that resolves the dependence on the historical data and tests compatibility with simultaneously measured competing channels.
status: Direct capture information has long been dominated by Weston and Todd's 1978 measurements [DOI:10.13182/NSE78-A27176]. CEA reported new measurements in 2026 that are undergoing analysis, so acquiring the data already constitutes a partial result toward independent replication.
solved_when: A completed analysis of the new CEA measurements is independently replicated, and an evaluation with quantified covariances is produced that resolves the reliance on the historical Weston–Todd dataset, including a compatibility test against simultaneously measured competing channels.
why: Sparse capture data currently limit the accuracy of isotope-inventory predictions involving 241Pu, which feed fuel-cycle and safeguards calculations.
key_works: L. W. Weston and J. H. Todd (1978), *Neutron Capture and Fission Cross Sections of Plutonium-241*, [DOI:10.13182/NSE78-A27176](https://doi.org/10.13182/NSE78-A27176); CEA (2026), [*Experimental challenges of nuclear reactions on plutonium-241*](https://irfu.cea.fr/en/Phocea/Vie_des_labos/Ast/ast.php?id_ast=5474&t=fait_marquant).

title: Americium-241 fast-energy capture uncertainty
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: How large is the neutron capture cross section of americium-241 at fast energies, and can the uncertainty there be substantially reduced through consistent differential measurements and evaluation? Any improvement should be demonstrated against independent validation, with normalization correlations treated properly.
status: This was an established NEA priority prior to the 2018 n_TOF publication (E. Mendoza et al., PhysRevC.97.054616). The thermal-data component of the request was completed in May 2022; the fast-energy component remains in progress per the OECD NEA HPRL status.
solved_when: The fast-energy capture uncertainty in the ranges identified by sensitivity studies is reduced via consistent differential measurements and an updated evaluation, and the improvement holds up under independent validation including normalization correlations.
why: The remaining gap propagates into inventories and irradiation predictions for americium-bearing civilian materials.
key_works: E. Mendoza et al. (2018), *Measurement and analysis of the 241Am neutron capture cross section at the n_TOF facility at CERN*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.97.054616](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.97.054616); OECD NEA, [HPRL status](https://cms.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_68808/95-am-241-n-g-n-tot).

title: Consistent gadolinium-155 and gadolinium-157 resonance evaluations
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Can gadolinium-155 and gadolinium-157 capture and transmission evaluations be made that jointly reproduce modern experiments and resolve the discrepant thermal values for both isotopes?
status: NEA requests were submitted in 2018; Mastromarco et al. (2019), *Cross section measurements of 155,157Gd(n,γ) induced by thermal and epithermal neutrons* ([DOI:10.1140/epja/i2019-12692-7](https://doi.org/10.1140/epja/i2019-12692-7)), supplied thermal and epithermal measurements. Subsequent work concerns evaluation and validation rather than wholly unmeasured reactions; see also the OECD NEA [request status](https://cms.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_68888/64-gd-155-n-g-n-tot).
solved_when: Evaluations for 155Gd and 157Gd exist that reproduce modern measurements, resolve the discrepant thermal values, meet the requested accuracy of roughly 4%, and carry independently validated covariance data.
why: These isotopes strongly influence gadolinium neutron-absorber behavior, so consistent evaluations directly affect the reliability of absorber modeling.
key_works: M. Mastromarco et al. (2019), *Cross section measurements of 155,157Gd(n,γ) induced by thermal and epithermal neutrons*, [DOI:10.1140/epja/i2019-12692-7](https://doi.org/10.1140/epja/i2019-12692-7); OECD NEA, [request status](https://cms.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_68888/64-gd-155-n-g-n-tot).

title: Iron-56 inelastic neutron–gamma channel closure
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Can the fast-energy neutron inelastic channel on 56Fe be made fully self-consistent, so that measured outgoing-neutron spectra, level-specific gamma production, and the total inelastic scattering cross section agree within a common evaluation? Resolving this requires identifying which transitions or reaction-model ingredients are currently missing and quantifying them in a published covariance evaluation.
status: A NEA high-priority request on this channel has remained active since 2008. The 2018 CIELO evaluation (M. Herman et al., [*Evaluation of Neutron Reactions on Iron Isotopes for CIELO and ENDF/B-VIII.0*](https://www.ornl.gov/publication/evaluation-neutron-reactions-iron-isotopes-cielo-and-endfb-viii0)) improved iron modeling, but state-resolved measurements and channel consistency remain active work (OECD NEA, [High Priority Request List](https://www.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_68746/hprlapp)).
solved_when: A common covariance evaluation of 56Fe inelastic scattering exists in which outgoing-neutron spectra, level-specific gamma production, and total inelastic cross sections are mutually consistent over the fast-energy range, with any missing transitions or model ingredients identified and documented.
why: Iron is ubiquitous in structural materials, shielding, and neutron diagnostics, so inconsistent 56Fe inelastic data propagates directly into uncertainty in reactor and facility calculations.
key_works: M. Herman et al. (2018), [*Evaluation of Neutron Reactions on Iron Isotopes for CIELO and ENDF/B-VIII.0*](https://www.ornl.gov/publication/evaluation-neutron-reactions-iron-isotopes-cielo-and-endfb-viii0); OECD NEA, [High Priority Request List](https://www.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_68746/hprlapp).

title: Early-time decay heat with separate beta and gamma benchmarks
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Can we build pulse-irradiation decay-heat benchmarks that separately resolve the beta (electron) and gamma (electromagnetic) components of the heat at short cooling times, rather than only the total? Such benchmarks would let evaluators pinpoint the specific decay-data errors behind any disagreement, instead of merely validating aggregate power.
status: Historical measurements and summation evaluations already provide substantial coverage of decay heat, but Nichols et al. (2023) identify persistent priorities for improvement and note that agreement in total power can conceal opposite beta and gamma errors.
solved_when: Independent pulse-irradiation measurements exist that resolve beta and gamma decay heat separately at early cooling times, and any disagreement with summation calculations is traced to identified decay-data errors rather than absorbed into agreement of the total heat.
why: Beta and gamma radiation deposit energy over different distances, so reactor and shielding calculations need separate predictions of each component; a match in total power can conceal compensating beta and gamma errors.
key_works: A. L. Nichols et al. (2023), *Improving fission-product decay data for reactor applications: part I—decay heat*, [DOI:10.1140/epja/s10050-023-00969-x](https://doi.org/10.1140/epja/s10050-023-00969-x).

title: Directly isolated uranium-238 antineutrino spectrum
open: Can the antineutrino spectrum from fast fission of uranium-238 be determined directly, with substantially reduced dependence on conversion methods and isotope-mixture assumptions, particularly at high energy? A solution requires either direct isolation of the spectrum or demonstrably identifiable multi-source inference, accompanied by a published covariance.
status: Haag et al. (2014) measured the beta spectrum from 238U fission products and converted it to an antineutrino spectrum, with uncertainty growing at high energy. A complementary direct-neutrino determination and improved precision remain open.
solved_when: A measurement of the 238U fast-fission antineutrino spectrum is available that is directly isolated (or inferred via a demonstrably identifiable multi-source method) with reduced conversion and isotope-mixture dependence, improved high-energy precision relative to Haag et al. (2014), and a published covariance.
why: Although the 238U contribution is the smaller component of reactor fission, it can still shape the high-energy reactor antineutrino spectrum, so its uncertainty propagates into reactor flux predictions and searches for new physics.
key_works: N. Haag et al. (2014), *Experimental Determination of the Antineutrino Spectrum of the Fission Products of 238U*, [arXiv:1312.5601](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.5601).

title: Reactor antineutrino spectrum below inverse-beta threshold
open: Can the reactor antineutrino spectrum below roughly 1.8 MeV — the inverse-beta-decay threshold — actually be measured? The goal is to reconstruct this subthreshold spectrum with a calibrated detector response, controlled backgrounds, and uncertainties that do not depend on assumed beta-decay summation calculations, and to determine which spectral features are identifiable through neutrino–nucleus recoil measurements.
status: Standard inverse-beta-decay measurements cannot access this region. CONUS+ observed coherent elastic antineutrino–nucleus scattering at a reactor in 2025 [N. Ackermann et al., *Direct observation of coherent elastic antineutrino–nucleus scattering*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09322-2], but an integrated recoil excess does not determine the full subthreshold source spectrum; unfolding the recoil spectrum to recover it is an ill-conditioned problem, and low-threshold dark-matter–style detectors are a relevant technique.
solved_when: A calibrated reconstruction of the subthreshold (≲ 1.8 MeV) reactor antineutrino spectrum is achieved with quantified, summation-independent uncertainties and demonstrated background control, including an assessment of which spectral features are identifiable from recoil data.
why: This would open a large, currently weakly tested portion of reactor beta-decay emission to direct experimental scrutiny, where the standard inverse-beta technique is entirely blind.
key_works: N. Ackermann et al. (2025), *Direct observation of coherent elastic antineutrino–nucleus scattering*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09322-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09322-2).

title: Correlation-aware criticality tallies
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: How can Monte Carlo criticality calculations deliver local power estimates and confidence intervals that stay calibrated in large, weakly coupled reactor models, where source clustering and population control introduce correlations? Formally, the goal is tallies whose coverage is demonstrably correct across independent calculations, including in spatially undersampled regions.
status: A decades-old Monte Carlo difficulty. Fröhlicher et al. demonstrated generational variance reduction on a one-speed slab in 2023 (arXiv:2301.03882); general reactor-scale guarantees remain a research target.
solved_when: Local power estimates with confidence intervals are produced that remain calibrated in a large, weakly coupled reactor model despite source clustering and population control, with coverage demonstrated across independent calculations including spatially undersampled regions.
why: Without it, apparently precise Monte Carlo calculations can conceal local statistical bias — reactor designers would trust confidence intervals that are wrong exactly where sampling is thinnest.
key_works: Fröhlicher et al. (2023), *Generational variance reduction in Monte Carlo criticality simulations as a way of mitigating unwanted correlations*, [arXiv:2301.03882](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.03882).

title: Affordable fully transient Monte Carlo
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Can a continuous-energy, three-dimensional Monte Carlo reactor transient be made an order of magnitude cheaper to simulate, without giving up verified uncertainty quantification and delayed-neutron physics? Formally, the goal is to reduce the computational cost of such transients by at least tenfold against a declared reference while retaining independently verified time-resolved uncertainty and delayed-neutron dynamics.
status: Fully transient Monte Carlo simulation is feasible today. The MC/DC 2024 release (Morgan et al., 2024, DOI:10.21105/joss.06415) and its 2023 initial-particle sampling methods (Variansyah et al., 2023, arXiv:2305.07646) supply current baselines, but coupled, long-duration transients remain computationally expensive.
solved_when: A continuous-energy, three-dimensional transient simulation achieves at least a tenfold reduction in computation time relative to a declared reference, with time-resolved uncertainty estimates that are independently verified and delayed-neutron dynamics retained.
why: It would make independent transient reference solutions cheap enough to be used routinely for validation of deterministic transient codes, rather than only in occasional benchmark campaigns.
key_works: Morgan et al. (2024), *Monte Carlo / Dynamic Code (MC/DC): An accelerated Python package for fully transient neutron transport and rapid methods development*, [DOI:10.21105/joss.06415](https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.06415); Variansyah et al. (2023), *An effective initial particle sampling technique for Monte Carlo reactor transient simulations*, [arXiv:2305.07646](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07646).

title: Positive, conservative adaptive low-rank transport
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Can a low-rank neutron transport scheme preserve both nonnegative flux and exact particle balance while adapting its rank through streaming regions, sharp material interfaces, and transients? In other words, is there an adaptive low-rank method for the transport equation with usable error bounds and these physical guarantees intact in realistic heterogeneous settings?
status: Kusch et al. established a low-rank criticality iteration and simplified convergence analysis in 2022, with demonstrated savings; however, the combined guarantees over realistic heterogeneous transients remain unestablished (Kusch, Whewell, McClarren, and Frank (2022), *A low-rank power iteration scheme for neutron transport criticality problems*, [arXiv:2201.12340](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12340)).
solved_when: An adaptive low-rank transport method is constructed that provably maintains nonnegative flux and particle balance, together with usable error bounds, through streaming, sharp material interfaces, and transient rank growth.
why: It would cut the memory cost of transport simulations without sacrificing physically meaningful solutions, since negative fluxes or broken particle balance render results unusable for reactor analysis.
key_works: Kusch, Whewell, McClarren, and Frank (2022), *A low-rank power iteration scheme for neutron transport criticality problems*, [arXiv:2201.12340](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12340).

title: Nonlinear uncertainty through depletion histories
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: How can correlated uncertainties — in nuclear data, flux, composition, and operating history — be propagated through repeated cycles of irradiation and cooling without relying on uncontrolled linearization? Formally, the challenge is a nonlinear uncertainty-quantification scheme whose accuracy can be validated against held-out isotope assays and residual-heat measurements.
status: Diez et al. (2015) showed that approximation choices and covariance libraries materially change burn-up uncertainty in PWR burn-up simulations (DOI:10.1016/j.anucene.2014.10.022). Full sampling supplies a costly baseline; efficient, reliable nonlinear propagation remains open.
solved_when: A propagation method is demonstrated that handles the full correlated uncertainty structure through repeated irradiation and cooling histories without uncontrolled linearization, and whose predicted residual-heat and isotope-inventory uncertainties are validated against held-out assay data.
why: It would make fuel-performance, storage, and waste-disposal predictions defensible rather than merely plausible, since current burn-up uncertainties are known to depend materially on the propagation method chosen.
key_works: Diez et al. (2015), *Comparison of nuclear data uncertainty propagation methodologies for PWR burn-up simulations*, [DOI:10.1016/j.anucene.2014.10.022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anucene.2014.10.022).

title: Identifiability limits of neutron-noise diagnosis
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Which combinations of core vibration, coolant fluctuations, and detector drift can produce identical readings on any realistic set of noisy neutron-noise detectors, and which can be told apart? The goal is a characterization of these indistinguishable source combinations, together with proven bounds or explicitly constructed experiments that separate the ambiguous causes.
status: The CORTEX project developed the relevant methods and controlled-reactor experiments during 2017–2021 (Demazière et al., 2017, [Noise-based core monitoring and diagnostics—Overview of the CORTEX project](https://research.chalmers.se/en/publication/253656)). The requested identifiability map does not yet exist as a named theorem; it is a proposed extension of that work.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the source combinations (vibration, coolant fluctuation, detector drift) that are indistinguishable from finite noisy detector measurements, backed either by proven bounds on distinguishability or by constructed experiments that separate the ambiguous causes.
why: It establishes exactly when noise-based localization of a perturbation is supported by the measured evidence and when the diagnosis instead requires additional sensors.
key_works: Demazière et al. (2017), [*Noise-based core monitoring and diagnostics—Overview of the CORTEX project*](https://research.chalmers.se/en/publication/253656).

title: Origin of bimodal intragranular gas bubbles
open: What physical mechanism produces the two distinct populations of nanometre-scale intragranular gas bubbles observed in UO₂ under irradiation? Formally: identify which combination of nucleation, dislocation trapping, coalescence, and irradiation-driven gas removal generates the bimodality, and predict both bubble-size distributions across temperature and fission rate without separately fitting each irradiation.
status: A decades-old microstructure question. A 2025 phase-field study (Jiajun Zhao et al., *Mesoscale simulation on bimodal distribution of nano-sized intragranular fission bubbles in UO₂*) reproduced the bimodality using gas re-solution, but alternative mechanisms remain experimentally distinguishable.
solved_when: A model that predicts both bubble populations across the full range of temperatures and fission rates of interest, with no irradiation-specific fitting, and whose mechanism is experimentally distinguishable from alternatives.
why: The bubble populations control swelling, gas retention, and subsequent fragmentation of the fuel, so resolving this underpins prediction of fuel behavior.
key_works: Jiajun Zhao et al. (2025), *Mesoscale simulation on bimodal distribution of nano-sized intragranular fission bubbles in UO₂*, [journal article](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167577X24019591).

title: Fission-spike gas re-solution law
open: Can we establish a transferable rate law describing how fission-fragment tracks return xenon from bubbles back into the fuel matrix? The law should capture the dependence on bubble size, track offset, energy deposition, and nearby dislocations, with independent gas inventories used to discriminate between thermal-spike and ballistic mechanisms.
status: Setyawan et al. (2018) parameterized atomistic re-solution in *Atomistic model of xenon gas bubble re-solution rate due to thermal spike in uranium oxide* ([DOI:10.1063/1.5042770](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5042770)); the conversion of electronic energy deposition into atomic heating remains a source of uncertainty in engineering-scale rates.
solved_when: A validated rate law exists that is transferable across conditions and reproduces independent gas inventory measurements, resolving whether re-solution proceeds via a thermal-spike or ballistic mechanism.
why: Incorrect re-solution rates propagate directly into swelling and gas-release predictions for reactor fuel.
key_works: W. Setyawan et al. (2018), *Atomistic model of xenon gas bubble re-solution rate due to thermal spike in uranium oxide*, [DOI:10.1063/1.5042770](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5042770).

title: Transient burst fission-gas release
open: Can the rapid release of fission gas that accompanies a power transient be predicted from microstructural measurements taken beforehand — in particular from grain-face cracks that open and heal? A successful theory should reproduce both the timing and the quantity of release in withheld transients, in regimes where ordinary diffusion contributes little.
status: Burst release has long resisted purely diffusional treatments. The OECD NEA benchmark of the Expert Group on Reactor Fuel Performance ([link](https://oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_70791/burst-fission-gas-release-fgr-benchmark-of-the-expert-group-on-reactor-fuel-performance-egrfp)) was designed to isolate short transients specifically to distinguish the burst mechanism from slower diffusion.
solved_when: A model, using only pre-transient microstructural characterization as input, quantitatively reproduces the release timing and released fraction observed in the benchmark's withheld transient cases.
why: Burst release directly changes internal rod pressure and fuel–cladding heat transfer during transients, so predicting it is a prerequisite for credible transient safety analysis.
key_works: OECD NEA, [*Burst Fission Gas Release Benchmark of the Expert Group on Reactor Fuel Performance*](https://oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_70791/burst-fission-gas-release-fgr-benchmark-of-the-expert-group-on-reactor-fuel-performance-egrfp).

title: Separating grain-size and diffusivity benefits of doped fuel
open: When does enlarging the fuel grain size improve fission-gas retention enough to outweigh the changes in xenon diffusivity caused by the dopant itself? The goal is a set of matched separate-effects irradiations in which grain size and chemical state are varied independently, capable of predicting both steady-state gas release and transient response.
status: Cooper et al. (2021) connected atomistic chemistry to engineering gas-release models for Cr₂O₃-doped UO₂, and the competing effects they identified motivate dedicated separate-effects irradiation studies, which have not yet been performed.
solved_when: Matched irradiations decoupling grain size from dopant-induced diffusivity changes exist, and the resulting data quantitatively predict steady-state release and transient response across the conditions tested.
why: Fuel qualification requires causal evidence that doped fuel performs better under specific conditions, rather than relying on correlations that conflate competing microstructural and chemical effects.
key_works: M. W. D. Cooper et al. (2021), *Fission gas diffusion and release for Cr₂O₃-doped UO₂: From the atomic to the engineering scale*, [DOI:10.1016/j.jnucmat.2020.152590](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2020.152590).

title: Metallic-fuel chemical attack of cladding
open: Can we predict how deeply a metallic fuel chemically attacks and weakens its cladding, given the interfacial reaction layers, the transported fission products, and the temperature history? The goal is a validated prediction of weakened cladding depth, tested at intermediate irradiation conditions and along full-length prototypic irradiated pins.
status: Salvato et al. (2024) compared two irradiated conditions in a SEM-EDS study of U-10Zr/HT-9 interaction and obtained useful model agreement, while identifying missing evidence at intermediate conditions and at prototypic pin lengths.
solved_when: A model quantitatively predicts chemically weakened cladding depth from interfacial layers, transported fission products, and temperature history, with predictions validated at intermediate conditions and along full-length irradiated fuel pins.
why: Chemical attack of the cladding can limit fuel lifetime even when bulk fuel swelling remains within acceptable limits, so reliable prediction is what separates a swelling-limited design margin from a hidden cladding-failure mechanism.
key_works: D. Salvato et al. (2024), *The effect of temperature and burnup on U-10Zr metallic fuel chemical interaction with HT-9: A SEM-EDS study*, [DOI:10.1016/j.jnucmat.2024.154928](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2024.154928).

title: Silver transport through apparently intact silicon carbide
open: How does silver manage to escape through TRISO fuel particles whose silicon carbide coatings appear microstructurally intact? A satisfactory theory must assign relative weights to grain boundaries, nanopore trapping, irradiation defects, and chemically assisted pathways, and predict release from independently characterized coating microstructures.
status: An enduring coated-fuel puzzle. AbdulHameed et al.'s 2025 preprint ([arXiv:2508.14325](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14325)) found that nanopore trapping was required to reconcile a grain-boundary transport model with measurements.
solved_when: A model quantifying the relative contributions of grain boundaries, nanopore trapping, irradiation defects, and chemically assisted pathways predicts measured silver release across independently characterized silicon carbide coating microstructures.
why: Silver release creates contamination and maintenance burdens for coated-fuel systems despite otherwise effective fission-product containment, so a predictive model would tell coating designers which microstructural features actually control escape.
key_works: M. AbdulHameed et al. (2025), *Modeling of silver transport in cubic SiC: Integrating molecular dynamics, bounds averaging, and uncertainty quantification*, [arXiv:2508.14325](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14325).

title: TRISO failure probabilities in the extreme tail
open: Can we predict the probability of failure of individual TRISO-coated fuel particles in the extreme tail of the distribution, starting from the joint statistics of coating geometry, manufacturing defects, material properties, and irradiation history? In particular, can such a framework handle correlated defects and non-spherical damage modes, and produce defensible tail estimates without extrapolating arbitrarily small failure rates from small samples that observed zero failures?
status: Jiang et al. (2021) implemented statistical failure analysis and multidimensional corrections in BISON, establishing the current modeling capability; validation of population-tail predictions beyond the tested configurations remains open.
solved_when: A validated predictive framework exists that quantifies extreme-tail failure probabilities for particle populations — accounting for correlated defects and non-spherical damage — and its predictions are validated against population-tail data beyond the configurations already tested, without relying on inference of tiny rates from zero-failure samples.
why: Whole-core fission product retention hinges on the rarest failures among enormous particle populations, so credible tail estimates are what actually determine whether retention requirements can be claimed.
key_works: W. Jiang et al. (2021), *TRISO particle fuel performance and failure analysis with BISON*, [DOI:10.1016/j.jnucmat.2021.152795](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2021.152795).

title: Late-life manganese–nickel–silicon precipitation
open: Can we predict precipitation and hardening in reactor pressure vessel steels over extended exposures where low flux, alloy composition, and thermal aging interact? More precisely, under what conditions does accelerated irradiation reproduce the precipitates and embrittlement seen in surveillance steels without empirical compensation?
status: Almirall et al. (2024) characterized nine commercial steels at extended-life fluences and tested models against them. Extrapolation across low-flux, long-duration histories remains a qualification problem.
solved_when: A physically grounded model predicts late-life Mn–Ni–Si precipitation and hardening across low-flux, long-duration exposure histories, validated against surveillance-steel microstructures and embrittlement, and accelerated irradiation is shown to reproduce those precipitates without empirical adjustment — closing the extrapolation/qualification gap.
why: These precipitates can change the usable lifetime of reactor vessels, so reliable prediction directly affects how long vessels may safely operate.
key_works: N. Almirall et al. (2024), *Irradiation microstructures and hardening in commercial nuclear reactor pressure vessel steels at high extended life fluence*, [primary article](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S258915292400053X).

title: When irradiation accelerates or suppresses salt corrosion
open: Does irradiation make intergranular corrosion in molten salts worse, better, or have no effect — and can we predict which? More precisely, the goal is to establish the conditions under which each sign holds, separating the roles of defect-enhanced alloy transport, radiolysis, and radiation-induced chemical-potential changes, and to validate that sign across radiation species and salt chemistries.
status: Zhou et al. (2019) observed proton irradiation decelerating intergranular corrosion of Ni–Cr alloys in molten salt, disproving the simple assumption that irradiation always worsens attack; the general operating boundaries for when irradiation accelerates, suppresses, or leaves corrosion unchanged remain open.
solved_when: A validated criterion exists that correctly predicts the sign of irradiation's effect on intergranular corrosion across radiation species and salt conditions, with defect-enhanced transport, radiolysis, and chemical-potential mechanisms separately identified and the sign experimentally confirmed in each regime.
why: Corrosion data from unirradiated coupon tests may misrepresent actual in-reactor wall loss, so reactor components could be either over-designed or — worse — under-designed against salt attack.
key_works: W. Zhou et al. (2019), *Proton Irradiation-Decelerated Intergranular Corrosion of Ni-Cr Alloys in Molten Salt*, [arXiv:1911.11798](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11798).

title: Irradiated silicon-carbide composite hermeticity
open: Can a complete silicon-carbide composite tube, including its joints and sealing layers, remain gas-tight throughout service under simultaneous heat flux, irradiation, and thermal cycling — and can its leakage be predicted from observable microcrack and joint damage? A formal statement would couple the evolving fracture state of the composite to measurable gas leakage and to the remaining lifetime of the sealing layer.
status: Koyanagi et al. (2024) found that radial-heat-flux irradiation could compromise the hermeticity of SiC/SiC composite tubes, while the monolithic SiC tubes tested under the same conditions retained theirs; they conclude that mitigation requires lifecycle validation.
solved_when: A validated, predictive relationship connects microcrack density and joint damage to measured gas leakage rates for complete composite tubes, and demonstrates hermeticity is maintained under combined radial heat flux, irradiation, and thermal cycling over the full component lifecycle.
why: Mechanical strength data alone cannot establish fission-product containment, so without a leakage-damage link there is no defensible basis for qualifying SiC composite tubing as a fission-product barrier.
key_works: T. Koyanagi et al. (2024), *Hermeticity of SiC/SiC composite and monolithic SiC tubes irradiated under radial high-heat flux*, [DOI:10.1016/j.jnucmat.2023.154784](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2023.154784).

title: Graphite dimensional turnaround across grades
open: Can we predict how a new, untested graphite grade behaves under irradiation — its initial shrinkage, the turnaround to expansion, and creep — purely from its as-manufactured pore and crystallite structure, with calibrated uncertainty that holds outside the set of measured grades and dose ranges?
status: Dhulipala et al. (2025) performed Bayesian calibration of four irradiated-property models across five graphite grades, including model discrepancy; out-of-grade and extended-dose prediction remains a stronger target beyond that work.
solved_when: A predictive model, calibrated on existing irradiation data, delivers shrinkage, turnaround, and creep predictions for grades and doses outside its calibration set, with quantified (calibrated) uncertainty bounds that are validated against withheld measurements.
why: Graphite dimensions and stiffness in the core evolve under irradiation, so reliable prediction of this turnaround governs how core geometry and load paths change over life — critical for structural safety margins in graphite-moderated reactors.
key_works: S. L. N. Dhulipala et al. (2025), *Bayesian calibration of irradiated graphite property models under high temperatures*, [DOI:10.1038/s41529-025-00710-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-025-00710-7).

title: Disturbance-wave control of intermittent dryout
open: Can we predict when local dry patches form and rewet in high-pressure annular steam–water flow — with spacers and nonuniform heating — directly from the statistics of disturbance waves? And can such predictions be transferred between fluids and geometries without refitting local closure models?
status: Morse et al. (2024) directly characterized intermittent dryout and proposed mechanistic models using a transparent refrigerant experiment (DOI:10.1016/j.ijheatmasstransfer.2023.124812); transferring these results to reactor conditions remains the narrower open problem.
solved_when: A validated predictive framework forecasts dry-patch formation and rewetting from disturbance-wave statistics under reactor-relevant conditions (high-pressure steam–water, spacers, nonuniform heating), and the framework transfers across fluids and geometries without refitting local closures.
why: Local dry patches, not wholesale film disappearance, govern the temperature excursions that threaten fuel and component integrity, so predicting them directly sets the margins for dryout mitigation.
key_works: R. W. Morse et al. (2024), *A new paradigm for the role of disturbance waves on film dryout and wall heat transfer in annular two-phase flow*, [DOI:10.1016/j.ijheatmasstransfer.2023.124812](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijheatmasstransfer.2023.124812).

title: Tenfold lower consumptive cooling water
subfield: Electricity systems, industrial heat, hydrogen, and water
open: Can a power plant reject heat using ten times less consumptive cooling water per net megawatt-hour than a conventional wet-cooled reference, without meaningfully hurting output or cost? Formally, the goal is a 10× reduction in annual consumptive cooling water per net MWh with no more than 5% annual output loss and no more than a 10% total levelized generation-cost premium, under the same climate and duty cycle.
status: Dry and hybrid cooling are known to reduce water demand but at cost and efficiency penalties. Existing adaptation studies, including Van Vliet et al. (2016), *Power-generation system vulnerability and adaptation to changes in climate and water resources*, [DOI:10.1038/nclimate2903](https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate2903), and IAEA (2024), [*Climate Change and Nuclear Power 2024*](https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/PUB9048_web.pdf), characterize the water–energy trade-off but do not establish this combined performance target.
solved_when: A demonstrated system achieves at least tenfold lower annual consumptive cooling water per net MWh relative to a wet-cooled reference under identical climate and duty cycle, while limiting annual output loss to ≤5% and the total levelized generation-cost premium to ≤10%.
why: It would free generators from water-constrained siting and reduce direct competition with other users during droughts.
key_works: Van Vliet et al. (2016), *Power-generation system vulnerability and adaptation to changes in climate and water resources*, [DOI:10.1038/nclimate2903](https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate2903); IAEA (2024), [*Climate Change and Nuclear Power 2024*](https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/PUB9048_web.pdf).

title: Subpercent predictive closure of uranium-235 antineutrino yield
open: Can the absolute antineutrino yield from uranium-235 fission be predicted to subpercent accuracy from independent fission and beta-decay data alone, in a way that is simultaneously consistent with direct neutrino measurements and aggregate electron measurements? The challenge is to resolve the remaining normalization discrepancies without tuning the prediction to the target neutrino yield itself.
status: The historical flux anomaly motivated renewed work from 2011 onward. Revised summation calculations improve agreement, but Perissé et al. (2023) still find incompatibility with legacy aggregate beta spectra and data-dominated uncertainties.
solved_when: A summation prediction built from independent fission and beta-decay data reproduces the absolute 235U antineutrino yield to subpercent accuracy while remaining consistent with direct neutrino measurements and aggregate beta (electron) spectra, with no fit of the predicted yield to the measured neutrino flux.
why: Accurate absolute yields are what make precision tests of neutrino properties and quantitative reactor monitoring possible; without closure, normalization ambiguities limit both.
key_works: L. Perissé et al. (2023), *A comprehensive revision of the summation method for the prediction of reactor antineutrino fluxes and spectra*, [arXiv:2304.14992](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14992).
